Dev log

Commander Wren

One commander leads on the Terra table: Wren, enhanced infantry on foot in powered armor, a scout drone hovering at her shoulder. She is the only commander on this battlefield — the red force opposing her is a commander-less mechanized column, richer and fielding an extra recon, whose only eyes are steel. Wren's gift is seeing the table before the enemy does. Her aura reaches 2 hexes: foot units inside it capture faster and hold cover like veterans.

Choose a board

Start a fresh battle on any board; the current battle is replaced. A saved battle always resumes on its own board.

How to play

Five boards against the CPU, on the miniature table.

Turn: tap one of your blue miniatures, tap a softly lit hex to move, then tap a red enemy in range: the segmented health bar above it previews the hit — the segments the shot would remove glow as a red ghost on the tail of its bar, and a second bar beneath shows the counterattack it would deal back the same way. Tap it again, or tap the crosshair beside it, to strike. Indirect units (Artillery, Rockets, deployed Siege) may move and fire in the same turn. The Siege must deploy in place before it can fire its long-range splash shot, and cannot move while deployed. Or skip the walking: with one of your units selected, tap a red enemy it could reach and shoot this turn and it closes to the best firing hex on its own — cheapest move first, then the best cover — and the forecast waits there for your confirming tap; if no legal move puts the shot on, the tap just inspects the enemy, as always. When every unit has acted, End Turn lights up. A unit whose only remaining choice is the checkmark is finished on its own: once it has moved and nothing but Wait (and maybe Undo) is left to it, it settles as acted without being asked — and a tower or held ruin turret with no enemy inside its firing band no longer holds the turn open either.

Capture: park Infantry, Mech or Wren herself on a property and choose Capture. Capturing takes two turns, faster inside Wren's aura. The clock is always visible: the Capture button says how many turns are left, the status bar repeats it for whoever is capturing (yours or the enemy's), and a small pennant on the property fills as the capture advances. Towns, factories and the relay pay income each turn; factories build new units. Capturing the enemy HQ wins at once. Units standing on their own towns, factories and HQ recover 2 HP at the start of their turn — repairs are free.

Win three ways: capture the enemy HQ, rout every enemy unit, or capture the central relay and hold it for 3 of your turns — that third way belongs to the Terra table; the other boards are won by HQ capture or rout.

Boards: five tables, chosen from the board picker on the start screen or the Boards list in the menu's Game section. Board 1 is the introductory Terra table, weighted a little toward Blue. Twin Bays adds water — impassable to ground units — crossed only by bridges. Pinewall is the forest-and-mountain fog table, its Old Ruin holding the central pass. Mare Dust is Luna: crater fields give forest cover and hiding, highlands stand in for hills, and neither army fields a copter in the thin air. The Belt is deep space: every unit is a ship, asteroid fields hide and cover like forest, dense clusters block movement and sight entirely, and stations — a Command Station, Docks and Habitats — replace towns, with a Precursor Derelict and its still-working turret at the centre.

Surround: each of your units standing beside the target beyond the first adds about +10% damage and blunts the counterattack. When a strike is armed, each supporting unit shows a gold marker, the target's outline deepens, and the damage ghost on the target's bar turns gold while the surround bonus is boosting the shot; a target whose whole bar pulses is about to be destroyed.

Fog: unexplored table lies in shadow, and sight on this table is short: most units see only 2 hexes, medium tanks and battle copters 3, and the recon — the army's dedicated eyes — 4. Explored ground stays dim and shows no units. Forest hides a unit unless an enemy stands next to it; hills and forests block sight lines. Finding the enemy before it finds you is the game: push recons and drones forward, and expect the red column to be doing the same with its recons. Wren's drones are the exception: whatever a drone can reach with its sensors is fully revealed, forest or no forest. One mercy for flyers: a shot at a copter or drone from ordinary ground fire has a 25% chance to miss entirely — anti-air guns, other aircraft, and the ruin turret's heavy shot never miss that way, and the forecast says so when the chance applies.

Commander Wren: only the blue army fields a commander. Wren is enhanced infantry on foot: she crosses forest, hills and rough ground at foot cost, takes infantry cover and forest hiding, is targeted as infantry rather than as a vehicle, can capture, and carries commander-grade firepower — she out-guns infantry and mechs outright and edges a tank against soft targets, though heavy armor still out-shoots her. Her aura reaches 2 hexes: foot units inside it capture faster, and infantry holding forest or a property inside it gains extra cover. If she is downed, she returns at her HQ after 3 turns at full strength, and while she is down no new drones can launch. She is built to grow with the campaign to come: each completed level will raise her maximum health by 2, up to 20 — in this battle she fights at 10, like everyone else. The red column has no commander, no aura and no drones — it compensates with extra funds and an extra recon.

Drones: tap Wren and choose Launch Drone; launching is her action for the turn. She may keep at most two drones aloft, and she carries four launches per battle in total — a lost drone does not refund one, and the button shows how many are left. A drone flies 6 hexes over any ground and cannot end its move on an occupied hex. Its sensors fully reveal everything within 3 hexes, including units hidden in forest, which makes it the best way to learn a new table. And it stings now: a light shot at range 1 (25 against infantry, less against armour), earning kill credit and veterancy like any unit. It is still fragile: a single solid hit from anything that can target air brings it down, and anti-air guns are its natural counter. As Wren gains levels in later battles, her drones will branch by your preference into offensive, defensive, repair and capture models.

Towers: Infantry, Mech and Wren can raise a tower for 1500 funds on plains, forest, hills or road. The builder becomes the tower's garrison and leaves the board as a separate piece: the army trades a unit for reach. A manned tower sees 3 hexes and can fire once a turn at range 2 with a mech-class shot, and enemies that strike it may be answered in kind. The garrison is safe while the tower stands; if the tower is destroyed, the garrison reappears on the hex at half strength, exhausted. Tap your tower and choose Unman Tower: the garrison steps out whole and rested next turn, but an unmanned tower goes dormant, seeing only its own hex and unable to fire, until a friendly foot unit steps in and mans it again. An enemy foot unit standing on your tower captures it over two turns, just like a property; when the capture completes, the tower changes hands and any garrison inside is thrown out at half strength. Towers cannot be automated yet; that upgrade arrives with later battles.

The Ruin: the Old Ruin at the table's heart is more than scenery. Its ancient amber turret is alive: while the ruin is neutral it fires on its own at anyone from either army who lingers in range 2–3. Infantry, Mech and Wren can capture the ruin like a property over two turns — stand on its hex beside the turret and choose Capture. Whoever holds the ruin gains +250 income a turn, and the turret changes allegiance with it. A held turret is aimed by its holder, exactly like a manned tower: on your turn, tap the turret and its targets in range 2–3 light up; tap one to see the forecast, tap again (or tap the crosshair) to fire. It gets one shot per round — and if you end your turn without firing it, it stays silent: manual means manual. The red army aims it the same way on its own turn. It can be re-captured the same way, and the turret flips with it, but a flip grants no extra shot: if it already fired this round, it cannot fire again until the next, whoever holds it. Its kills are credited to whoever holds it.

Veterans: units earn experience and rank chevrons (about +10% damage per rank) and keep a personal kill count, shown with a skull badge. Drone kills credit the shooter; tower kills credit the tower.

Forgiveness: a unit that has only moved can undo its move with the Undo Move button in the action panel. A move that reveals new ground or a hidden enemy cannot be taken back. The battle saves itself as you play; resume it from the menu's Game section.

Inspecting the table: tap any hex and the status bar fixed at the bottom of the screen shows that hex's terrain on the left and, when a unit or tower you can see stands there, its full details on the right. The bar is permanent and the map fills exactly the space above it, so no hex or unit is ever hidden behind it. The table is larger than the map area and drags to pan in every direction; the menu (top-right) holds the objectives with live progress, sound settings, these rules, kill counts, the battle log and game controls, so the table itself stays clear.
